lessons.title: Toxicology: toxidromes, cardiotoxic poisonings & special resuscitation
lessons.summary: Toxicology management starts with supportive ABC, glucose/temperature/ECG, pattern recognition and consultation—not antidote memorization alone.

sections.title: 1) Toxidrome approach
paragraphs: Sympathomimetic, anticholinergic, cholinergic, opioid, sedative-hypnotic and serotonin syndromes provide pattern recognition, but mixed ingestions are common.

sections.title: 2) ECG in poisoning
paragraphs: QRS widening, QT prolongation, AV block/bradycardia and ventricular dysrhythmia can guide urgency and toxin class. Sodium-channel blockers, TCAs and some antiarrhythmics are classic QRS-widening causes.

sections.title: 3) Supportive priorities
paragraphs: Airway/ventilation, seizure control, temperature, glucose, fluids/vasopressors and continuous ECG are often more important than a specific antidote early.

sections.title: 4) 2025 AHA special circumstances
paragraphs: Updated guidance covers opioid, beta-blocker, calcium-channel blocker, cocaine/sympathomimetic, cyanide, digoxin, local anesthetic systemic toxicity, methemoglobinemia, organophosphate/carbamate, sodium-channel blocker and hydrocarbon poisoning.

sections.title: 5) CCB poisoning example
paragraphs: 2025 AHA: high-dose insulin and vasopressors are recommended for hypotension in life-threatening CCB poisoning; calcium is reasonable, while glucagon usefulness is uncertain.

key_points: ECG is a toxicology vital sign
Call poison center/toxicology early when available

research_updates.title: Special circumstances guideline expansion
research_updates.takeaway: AHA 2025 updated 44 recommendations and added 140 new recommendations across special circumstances including multiple poisonings and pregnancy.

quiz.q: Life-threatening CCB poisoning with hypotension: 2025 AHA recommends?
quiz.explain: High-dose insulin and vasopressors are recommended for hypotension in life-threatening CCB poisoning.

lessons.title: Acetaminophen/Paracetamol Poisoning: Silent Early, Dangerous Later
lessons.summary: ผู้ป่วยอาจดูดีช่วงแรกแต่เกิด hepatic failure ภายหลัง—timing and dose history matter.

sections.title: 1) Toxic mechanism
paragraphs: Excess dose saturates normal metabolism and increases toxic NAPQI formation; glutathione depletion leads to hepatic injury.

sections.title: 2) History
paragraphs: Clarify exact product, strength, number taken, time, repeated supratherapeutic use, co-ingestants and body weight. Combination products are common.

sections.title: 3) Evaluation
paragraphs: A timed serum concentration is interpreted with appropriate nomogram only for eligible acute single ingestions; repeated/unknown-time ingestion needs a different strategy. Liver tests and metabolic markers matter in delayed presentation.

sections.title: 4) Antidote
paragraphs: N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and is most effective when started early, but can benefit later toxicity. Exact initiation/route/regimen follows poison center/local protocol.

prehospital_focus: Contact poison center/medical control early for significant ingestion
pitfalls: Reassurance because patient is asymptomatic early
Using nomogram for repeated or unknown-time ingestion

lessons.title: Salicylate Poisoning: Hyperventilation Is Protective
lessons.summary: tachypnea is often compensation; intubation that reduces minute ventilation can precipitate abrupt deterioration.

sections.title: 1) Acid-base physiology
paragraphs: Salicylates stimulate respiratory center → respiratory alkalosis, while mitochondrial toxicity produces metabolic acidosis. As pH falls, more nonionized salicylate enters CNS.

sections.title: 2) Clinical clues
paragraphs: Tinnitus, nausea/vomiting, diaphoresis, tachypnea, fever, altered mental status and pulmonary edema. Chronic toxicity can be subtle, especially in older adults.

sections.title: 3) Airway danger
paragraphs: If intubation becomes unavoidable, losing the patient’s high minute ventilation or allowing acidemia can rapidly increase CNS salicylate. Expert planning is crucial.

sections.title: 4) Definitive concepts
paragraphs: Alkalinization and, in severe cases, hemodialysis are key hospital therapies. Serial levels and clinical status are more informative than one concentration.

lessons.title: TCA & Sodium-Channel Blocker Toxicity: QRS Is a Warning Sign
lessons.summary: cardiotoxicity from sodium-channel blockade can cause wide QRS, hypotension, seizure and ventricular dysrhythmia.

sections.title: 1) Mechanism
paragraphs: Fast sodium-channel blockade slows phase-0 depolarization and conduction; TCAs also have anticholinergic and alpha-blocking effects.

sections.title: 2) ECG clues
paragraphs: QRS widening, terminal R in aVR and ventricular dysrhythmia support sodium-channel toxicity but ECG must be interpreted clinically.

sections.title: 3) Sodium bicarbonate
paragraphs: Hypertonic sodium load/alkalinization is a central therapy for significant TCA/sodium-channel blocker cardiotoxicity according to toxicology guidance.

sections.title: 4) Seizure/shock
paragraphs: Treat seizures promptly, support ventilation and perfusion, and obtain toxicology/poison-center guidance for refractory cases.

lessons.title: Beta-Blocker & Calcium-Channel Blocker Poisoning
lessons.summary: bradycardic shock from cardiotoxic drugs requires physiology-driven antidotal and vasoactive care.

sections.title: 1) Phenotypes
paragraphs: Beta-blockers often cause bradycardia, hypotension and reduced contractility; some have sodium-channel or CNS effects. CCBs can cause vasodilation, bradycardia/conduction delay and hyperglycemia (especially severe CCB toxicity).

sections.title: 2) Immediate stabilization
paragraphs: Airway/ventilation, ECG, glucose, perfusion and early poison-center consultation. Conventional atropine may be insufficient in severe poisoning.

sections.title: 3) High-dose insulin concept
paragraphs: AHA 2025 special-circumstances guidance supports high-dose insulin therapy in life-threatening CCB poisoning, with vasopressors and consideration of calcium. This requires intensive glucose/potassium monitoring and protocolized dosing.

sections.title: 4) Refractory shock
paragraphs: Multiple therapies may be required, including vasopressors/inotropes and advanced mechanical support in selected centers.

research_updates.title: AHA Special Circumstances: cardiotoxic poisoning
research_updates.takeaway: Updated AHA resuscitation guidance includes high-dose insulin and vasoactive support for life-threatening calcium-channel blocker poisoning.

lessons.title: Opioid Toxicity: Ventilation First, Naloxone to Restore Breathing
lessons.summary: เป้าหมายคือ oxygenation/ventilation และ reversal ของ dangerous respiratory depression ไม่ใช่ทำให้ตื่นเต็มที่ทุกคน.

sections.title: 1) Toxidrome
paragraphs: CNS depression, slow/absent respirations and miosis are classic but pupils can vary. Synthetic opioids may be potent and co-ingestants common.

sections.title: 2) Immediate priority
paragraphs: Open airway and ventilate with BVM/oxygen when breathing is inadequate. Do not wait for naloxone to work before supporting ventilation.

sections.title: 3) Naloxone strategy
paragraphs: Titrate according to protocol to restore adequate spontaneous ventilation. Larger/repeated doses may be needed with potent opioids; abrupt full withdrawal can cause agitation/vomiting.

sections.title: 4) Re-sedation
paragraphs: Naloxone duration may be shorter than the opioid; observe for recurrent respiratory depression and consider long-acting/extended-release exposures.

lessons.title: Organophosphate/Carbamate Poisoning: Cholinergic Crisis
lessons.summary: secretions + bronchospasm + weakness make airway management central; atropine endpoint is pulmonary drying/improved ventilation.

sections.title: 1) Cholinergic excess
paragraphs: Muscarinic findings include bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, bradycardia, vomiting/diarrhea, urination, sweating and miosis. Nicotinic effects include fasciculations, weakness and paralysis.

sections.title: 2) Decontamination safety
paragraphs: Protect rescuers from secondary contamination; remove contaminated clothing and decontaminate according to hazmat/poison protocol.

sections.title: 3) Atropine goal
paragraphs: Atropine is titrated to control life-threatening muscarinic effects—especially bronchial secretions/bronchospasm and ventilation—not to normalize pupil size.

sections.title: 4) Oxime/benzodiazepine
paragraphs: Pralidoxime and seizure treatment may be indicated depending on agent/severity/protocol.

lessons.title: Alcohol Withdrawal: From Tremor to Delirium Tremens
lessons.summary: autonomic hyperactivity can progress to seizures and delirium; do not overlook hypoglycemia, trauma or infection.

sections.title: 1) Spectrum
paragraphs: Tremor, anxiety, nausea, diaphoresis, tachycardia and hypertension can begin after reduction/cessation. Withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens are severe manifestations.

sections.title: 2) Differential
paragraphs: Head injury, sepsis, hypoglycemia, hepatic encephalopathy, toxic ingestion and psychiatric disease may coexist.

sections.title: 3) Treatment principle
paragraphs: Benzodiazepines are standard first-line therapy for clinically significant withdrawal in most protocols; severe cases need repeated assessment and airway monitoring.

sections.title: 4) Nutrition/metabolic issues
paragraphs: Chronic alcohol use raises concern for thiamine deficiency, electrolyte disorders and malnutrition; check glucose promptly.
